content: The sensitivity and specificity of various diagnostic tools for tuberculosis (TB) were evaluated in different settings. For individuals presenting with any cough, the sensitivity ranged from 40% to 74%, and the specificity ranged from 69% to 90%. In settings with low HIV prevalence, the sensitivity for detecting any TB symptom was 58% to 82%, with a specificity of 35% to 87%. In high HIV prevalence settings, the sensitivity increased to 76% to 93%, with a specificity of 53% to 95%. When combining both low and high HIV prevalence settings, the sensitivity was 68% to 86%, and the specificity was 50% to 85%. The diagnostic yield of different screening and diagnostic algorithms was estimated using pooled sensitivity and specificity data from systematic reviews. These included tools such as the Xpert MTB/RIF test and sputum-smear microscopy, with culture-confirmed pulmonary TB serving as the gold standard. The sensitivity and specificity of clinical diagnosis, which involves clinical evaluation and chest radiography for smear-negative TB patients, were derived from an economic evaluation study. This study utilized data from a demonstration of the Xpert MTB/RIF test conducted in three countries. For diagnostic tests, liquid culture (the gold standard) demonstrated 100% sensitivity and specificity. Conventional sputum-smear microscopy showed a sensitivity of 31% to 89% and a specificity of 93% to 100%. The Xpert MTB/RIF test had a sensitivity of 70% to 100% and a specificity of 91% to 100%. Clinical diagnosis, which includes chest radiography after negative sputum-smear microscopy or Xpert MTB/RIF, had a sensitivity of 10% to 51% and a specificity of 79% to 97%. In children, the presence of symptoms such as cough, fever, weight loss, or fatigue had a sensitivity of 76% and a specificity of 77%, with a positive predictive value of 33% and a negative predictive value of 96%. In HIV-positive children, symptoms like cough lasting more than two weeks, fever, or failure to thrive had a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 59%. The absence of these symptoms had a negative predictive value of 99%. A systematic review summarized the number needed to screen (NNS) to detect one case of TB in various risk groups. For the general population, the NNS varied widely depending on TB incidence rates, ranging from 137 to 30,865 in low-incidence settings and from 16 to 6,355 in high-incidence settings. Specific risk groups, such as healthcare workers, prisoners, and people living with HIV, had lower NNS values, reflecting higher TB prevalence in these populations. The acceptability of TB screening was influenced by factors such as the invasiveness of the test, the time required for testing and follow-up, perceived negative consequences (e.g., legal or social), incentives offered, and the quality of interaction with healthcare providers. Simple, non-invasive, point-of-care TB screening methods were generally more acceptable than complex or invasive procedures. Acceptability tended to decline with repeated screening over time, suggesting that the frequency of screening should balance health benefits against the risk of refusal. Screening for active TB has the potential to improve health outcomes by enabling earlier treatment initiation, reducing the risk of poor treatment outcomes, and mitigating long-term socioeconomic consequences. However, the impact of systematic screening on TB transmission remains uncertain due to gaps in understanding the natural history of TB, including the timing of transmission events and the progression of TB symptoms. The effectiveness of screening in reducing transmission may depend on the stage at which smear positivity develops and the accessibility of healthcare services for symptomatic individuals.
